abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has revolutionized treatment for relapsed/refractory B-cell malignancies, including B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (B-ALL) and Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). However, the influence of obesity and related comorbidities on treatment outcomes and toxicity profiles remains unclear. This retrospective study included 115 patients treated with CAR-T therapy at Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology from 2017 to October 2023. Patients were stratified into high-risk and low-risk groups based on Body Mass Index (BMI) and the presence of obesity-related comorbidities. Clinical outcomes, including Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) and Immune effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome (ICANS) severity, treatment efficacy, Overall Survival (OS), and Progression-Free Survival (PFS), were analyzed. Logistic regression models assessed the relationships between covariates and clinical outcomes. The median BMI was 21.91 (IQR 19.265–24.365). Among the patients, 32 were overweight, and only one had a BMI over 30. Severe CRS occurred in 16 patients, with a higher proportion in those with obesity or related conditions (10.4% vs. 3.5%, p = 0.01). Hyperlipidemia significantly increased the risk of severe CRS (OR = 3.730, CI [1.204–11.556], p = 0.022). However, being overweight, having diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, or fatty liver were not significantly associated with severe CRS. Elevated total cholesterol was moderately correlated with increased Interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels (R = 0.637, p < 0.001) and weakly with Interferon gamma (IFN-γ) (R = 0.337, p < 0.001). Besides, overweight patients had a lower proportion of CAR-T cells post-infusion (OR = 0.98, CI [0.961–1.0], p = 0.048). Obesity and related comorbidities did not significantly impact treatment efficacy. However, hyperlipidemia was associated with an increased risk of severe CRS, emphasizing the need for tailored risk management strategies in CAR-T therapy. Clinical trial: NCT02965092/ NCT03366350/ NCT04008251(ClinicalTrials.gov).

sec.p: Keywords: CAR-T therapy, Obesity, Hyperlipidemia, B-cell malignancies, Cytokine release syndrome
Received 2024 Dec 29; Accepted 2025 Mar 24; Issue date 2025.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has revolutionized the treatment landscape for relapsed/refractory (R/R) B-cell malignancies, including B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (B-ALL) [1] and Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) [2]. As the clinical application of CAR-T therapy expands, understanding the variables that influence its efficacy and safety is critical. Previous research primarily focused on the primary disease and the CAR-T cells themselves [3–6]. However, as the management of CAR-T therapy becomes standardized, individual differences such as race, BMI, age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, organ function, and metabolic function are increasingly receiving attention [7]. Among these, obesity and its related underlying diseases emerge as a factor that may affect the treatment outcomes and toxicity profiles in patients undergoing this innovative treatment.

Obesity, defined by an elevated BMI, is a growing global health concern. It is often associated with metabolic disorders such as hyperlipidemia, hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, and fatty liver, which collectively contribute to a pro-inflammatory state known as metaflammation [8]. Recent studies from the West (USA and Germany) have begun to explore the relationship between BMI and the outcomes of CAR-T cell therapy, with mixed results regarding its impact on efficacy and adverse events such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) [7, 9, 10]. The diverse findings suggest that the interplay between patient body composition and CAR-T therapy outcomes is complex and warrants further investigation. However, no study has yet focused on the Chinese population.

Moreover, the implications of BMI on CAR-T therapy outcomes extend beyond clinical responses and toxicities. Obesity is a condition accompanied by various metabolic and inflammatory changes, which could potentially interact with CAR-T cell dynamics [10, 11]. Understanding these interactions is essential for tailoring CAR-T therapy, improving patient outcomes, and mitigating adverse effects.

In light of these considerations, this paper aims to investigate the influence of obesity and related underlying diseases on the severity of CRS and the efficacy of CAR-T therapy in treating B-cell malignancies. By evaluating the correlation between body composition, metabolic profiles, and clinical outcomes, we seek to provide insights that can inform personalized treatment strategies and enhance the safety and effectiveness of CAR-T therapy.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study was conducted at Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. The study period extended from 2017 to October 2023, during which more than 500 patients received CAR-T therapy. Among them, patients were included based on the following criteria: First, diagnosis of B-ALL or DLBCL. Second, treatment with CAR-T therapy. Third, availability of complete medical records.

Data were retrospectively collected from patient medical records and included: age, gender, BMI, presence of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, fatty liver, incidence and severity of CRS and ICANS, treatment efficacy (complete response, partial response, stable disease, progressive disease), overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and the proportion of CAR-T cells in the patient's peripheral blood on the 14th day after CAR-T infusion.

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Institutional Review Board of Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology Union Hospital. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legal guardians.

sec.title: Outcome measures
sec.p: CRS and ICANS were graded according to the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) criteria [12]. CRS severity was categorized into grades 0–5, with 3 or higher grades indicating severe symptoms. ICANS severity was similarly categorized. Treatment response was assessed using standard response criteria for B-cell malignancies [13]. The categories included complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD), and progressive disease (PD). OS was defined as the time from CAR-T infusion to the date of death from any cause. PFS was defined as the time from CAR-T infusion to the date of disease progression or death (https://www.nccn.org/guidelines).

sec.title: Detailed data analysis
sec.p: Patients were stratified into high-risk and low-risk groups based on their BMI and the presence of obesity-related comorbid conditions. The high-risk group included patients with a BMI greater than 24 and/or any obesity-related underlying disease. The low-risk group comprised patients without these risk factors. Peak levels of key cytokines, including IL-6 and IFNγ, CRP, and ferritin, were measured to investigate their relationship with CRS and ICANS severity.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient baseline characteristics and clinical outcomes. Continuous variables were expressed as median (interquartile range), and categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Logistic regression models assessed the relationship between covariates (BMI, comorbid conditions) and clinical outcomes (CRS severity, treatment efficacy). All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.2). A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Description of the cohort.
sec.p: A total of 115 patients were included in the study, with a median age of 43 years (interquartile range: 29 to 57 years). The cohort comprised 57 patients with DLBCL and 58 patients with B-ALL. Prior to CAR-T cell infusion, 42 patients (36.5%) were diagnosed with refractory disease, and 54 patients (47%) had experienced at least one relapse. Following the infusion, 72 patients developed CRS of varying severity, with 16 cases classified as severe CRS. ICANS was observed in 9 patients, with 3 cases being severe. To date, 26 patients in the cohort have died, and 45 patients have relapsed post-infusion. The median OS for the cohort was 7 months (interquartile range: 2 to 16 months), and the median PFS was 4 months (interquartile range: 1 to 12 months).

The median BMI of the 115 patients was 21.91, with an interquartile range of 19.265 to 24.365 (Table 1). Among them, 32 patients were classified as overweight (BMI ≥ 24), and only one patient had a BMI greater than 30. There were 26 cases of hyperlipidemia, 13 cases of hypertension, 9 cases of diabetes, and 8 cases each of coronary heart disease and fatty liver. Patients were divided into high-risk and low-risk groups based on their BMI and the presence of obesity-related comorbidities. The high-risk group included 53 patients with a BMI greater than 24 and/or any obesity-related underlying disease, while the low-risk group comprised 62 patients without these risk factors.

sec.title: Obesity and its related underlying diseases do not significantly impact the treatment efficacy.
sec.p: The overall response rate (ORR) to CAR-T therapy was 76.5%, with 66.1% of patients achieving a CR and 10.4% achieving a PR (Table 2). The treatment efficacy was not significantly different between the high-risk and low-risk groups (p = 0.75). Both groups showed comparable rates of CR, PR, SD and PD. The median follow-up period was 24 months. During this period, the OS and PFS were analyzed. The OS rates at 12 and 24 months were 37.4% and 11.3%, respectively. The PFS rates at 12 and 24 months were 26.1% and 5.2%, respectively. There were no significant differences in OS or PFS between the high-risk and low-risk groups.

sec.title: Hyperlipidemia was associated with severe CRS.
sec.p: Of the 115 patients, 73 experienced varying degrees of adverse reactions (Table 2). There was no correlation between obesity or the presence of related underlying diseases and the occurrence of adverse reactions (p = 0.89). However, among the 16 patients who experienced severe adverse reactions, the proportion of those who were obese or had any related underlying condition was significantly higher (10.4% vs. 3.5%, p = 0.01). All 16 patients developed severe CRS, and among them, 2 patients experienced grade 5 CRS, both of whom were obese. 3 patients developed severe ICANS, but there was no significant difference in obesity levels among these patients.

Logistic regression analysis was performed on the 115 patients, grouping them by obesity or the presence of underlying diseases and examining the occurrence of severe CRS (Fig. 1). It was found that patients with hyperlipidemia were more likely to develop severe CRS (OR = 3.730, 95%CI [1.204—11.556], p = 0.022). However, being overweight, having diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, or fatty liver were not significantly associated with the occurrence of severe CRS. For patients with obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, there appears to be a trend towards an increased risk of CRS. However, the results are not statistically significant (OR for obese patients = 2.625, 95% CI: 0.864—7.971, p = 0.089; OR for diabetic patients = 2.044, 95% CI: 0.383—10.914, p = 0.403; OR for hypertensive patients = 2.250, 95% CI: 0.542—9.345, p = 0.264). Additionally, the impacts of coronary heart disease and fatty liver on the occurrence of severe CRS are not statistically significant, with p-values greater than 0.9.

caption.p: Forest plots of obesity related characteristics with severe CRS. ORs were calculated from simple (univariate) logistic regression models with intercept term. Interval bands represent 95% CIs for the point estimates. Arrowheads indicate CI extending beyond axis range. Overweight defined as BMI ≥ 24

sec.p: The correlation analysis between total cholesterol, triglycerides, and CRS-related biomarkers (IL-6, IFN-γ, ferritin, CRP) revealed that elevated total cholesterol levels are significantly positively correlated with increased IL-6 and IFN-γ levels. There is a moderate correlation with IL-6 (R = 0.637, p < 0.001) and a weak correlation with IFN-γ (R = 0.337, p < 0.001) (Fig. 2), while no significant correlations were found with CRP and ferritin (p = 0.102 and p = 0.1, respectively). Triglycerides showed no significant correlation with any of the four inflammatory biomarkers, and all R values were below 0.3.

The graphical inset depicts the Spearman correlation coefficient with a positive R-value indicating a positive correlation and a negative R-value indicating a negative correlation, as well as the respective p-value. The 95% CI bands of the best-fit line from the simple linear regression are shown in light shading

sec.title: The proportion of CAR-T cells of overweight patients was significantly reduced.
sec.p: The CAR-T cell infusion dose for patients was 5 (2–6) × 10^6/kg, with the proportion of CAR-T cells in the infusion product being 32.5% (21.3%−42.1%). On the 14th day following CAR-T infusion, the proportion of CAR-T cells in the patients' peripheral blood was 38.9% (21.8%−45.7%). When patients were stratified based on obesity or the presence of underlying diseases, it was observed that overweight patients had a significantly lower proportion of CAR-T cells post-infusion (OR = 0.98, 95%CI [0.961, 1.0], p = 0.048) (Fig. 3). In contrast, obesity, hypertension, coronary heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and fatty liver did not show significant correlations with CAR-T cell expansion dynamics.

Interval bands represent 95% CIs for the point estimates. Arrowheads indicate CI extending beyond axis range. Overweight defined as BMI ≥ 24

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Although the prevalence of obesity and related comorbidities among Chinese patients in this study is relatively low, our findings still suggest that obesity increases the severity of CRS in patients undergoing CAR-T therapy. The pro-inflammatory state associated with obesity, indicated by elevated baseline levels of inflammatory markers like IL-6 and IFN-γ, likely contributes to this exacerbated response. This relationship suggests that the systemic inflammation common in obese patients amplifies the cytokine cascade initiated by CAR-T cell activation, resulting in more intense inflammatory symptoms. The link between obesity and enhanced CRS severity is supported by Subklewe et al.[10], who noted that body composition correlated with increased CRS intensity, specifically visceral adipose tissue (VAT), on the onset and severity of CRS. VAT is known to be metabolically active and secretes a variety of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, IFN-γ, and IL-1β. These cytokines can contribute to a state of chronic low-grade inflammation known as "metaflammation," which is common in obesity [14, 15]. VAT acts almost like an endocrine organ, not just influencing but also interacting with the immune system [16]. Adipokines released from VAT can influence immune cell function and cytokine production, creating feedback loops that enhance inflammatory responses [17]. Moreover, IL-8, a pro-inflammatory chemokine, is frequently elevated in obese individuals and is associated with metabolic inflammation and the recruitment of immune cells. TNF-α, a key mediator of chronic inflammation in obesity, contributes to metabolic dysregulation and endothelial dysfunction. Elevated levels of IL-8 and TNF-α may exacerbate the inflammatory responses observed in CRS. Meanwhile, IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine, is paradoxically dysregulated in obesity. Some studies suggest that obesity may impair the regulatory function of IL-10, leading to an imbalance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory responses during CRS [18]. This interaction can amplify the effects of the infused CAR-T cells, precipitating an earlier and more severe CRS. Overall, regardless of whether in Asian or European populations, obesity impacts the immune function and metabolism within the tumor microenvironment to some extent, thereby playing a pro-inflammatory role.

Given the limited number of ICANS cases in this cohort, the study did not extensively explore the influence of obesity on neurotoxic effects. However, obesity is a pro-inflammatory state that may influence neurotoxicity through several mechanisms. Previous studies suggest that obesity is associated with increased systemic inflammation and metabolic dysregulation, characterized by elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-α, which can impair the integrity of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) [19]. Also, obesity has been linked to chronic neuroinflammation and microglial activation, which may predispose patients to more severe ICANS symptoms [20]. Notably, previous research by the Mayo Clinic has examined the impact of age on ICANS in patients with DLBCL treated with axicabtagene Ciloleucel [21]. The study was particularly focused on comparing how older and younger patients differ in terms of the presentation, progression, and management of ICANS. The research suggested that age did not appear to significantly impact the clinical presentation or short-term outcomes of ICANS following CAR T-cell therapy. This conclusion helps in understanding that older patients can be considered for CAR T-cell therapies with a similar expectation of risk for neurotoxicity as younger patients [22], providing valuable information for treatment planning and risk assessment.

In contrast to severe side effects, obesity does not significantly impact treatment efficacy or prognosis, aligning with findings from prior research[9]. There is no direct mechanism by which obesity is known to impair the mechanisms of action of CAR-T cells, such as antigen recognition, T-cell receptor signaling, or the cytotoxic action of these cells. Notably, researchers suggest that cholesterol metabolism might influence immune cell function within the tumor microenvironment of solid tumors [23, 24]. This is attributed to a disparity in cholesterol levels, where T cells exhibit a deficiency, while immunosuppressive bone marrow cells and tumor cells display an abundance of cholesterol. This imbalance impedes T cell proliferation and could lead to autophagy-mediated apoptosis, particularly affecting cytotoxic T cells. But in hematologic malignancies, unless the obesity is severe enough to cause significant issues such as hypoxia or severely altered blood chemistry, the basic functions of engineered T cells might not be impaired. This could be due to the highly individual nature of both obesity and cancer, where other factors such as the type of cancer, the specific construct of the CAR-T cell, and individual patient health profiles play more critical roles [25, 26]. Moreover, patients undergoing CAR-T therapy are closely monitored and receive supportive care [27–29] that may mitigate some of the potential negative impacts of obesity on general health and immune function, thereby preserving the efficacy of the therapy.

Previous research often did not differentiate the impact of obesity on CAR-T cell kinetics and inflammatory responses distinctly, which our study has highlighted. Our results revealed that obese patients exhibited a modified kinetic profile of CAR-T cells, which manifested as a reduced overall expansion compared to non-obese patients. This finding could be attributed to the altered metabolic and inflammatory environment in obese individuals, which might interfere with CAR-T cell proliferation and function [30]. Obese patients often have higher cholesterol levels, and cholesterol is an essential component of cell membranes and influences how immune cells communicate and respond to signals. Excess cholesterol can disrupt T-cell signaling pathways, potentially reducing CAR-T cell proliferation [31]. Besides, obesity is associated with chronic low-grade inflammation, characterized by elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF-α. These cytokines can drive T-cell exhaustion, making CAR-T cells less effective at expanding and persisting. Adipokines, signaling molecules secreted by fat cells, may also influence immune responses. Some adipokines promote inflammation, which could negatively impact CAR-T cell function [18]. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for optimizing CAR-T cell dosing and timing strategies to enhance efficacy and reduce adverse effects in obese patients. Additionally, literature cited in earlier studies have shown variability in the pharmacokinetics and dynamics of CAR-T cells among different patient groups [7, 32], but without a specific focus on obese populations. Our findings fill this gap by specifically addressing how obesity modifies these dynamics, which is crucial for tailoring treatment protocols to individual patient needs.

Given the significant influence of obesity on the severity of CRS and the dynamics of CAR-T cell expansion, clinicians must consider these factors when planning CAR-T therapy. Modifying lymphodepleting chemotherapy dosages and optimizing CAR-T cell dosing [33] according to individual patient profiles can help manage increased risks associated with obesity. Early intervention strategies for CRS management [34], particularly tailored to the inflammatory profiles of obese patients, could also be crucial. Moreover, the insights into CAR-T cell kinetics[35] and related CRS provided by our study should encourage the development of personalized CAR-T cell infusion schedules that account for a patient’s body composition, potentially improving therapeutic outcomes and reducing toxicity.

Our study enhances the understanding of how obesity affects the dynamics and clinical outcomes of CAR-T therapy, emphasizing the need for personalized treatment approaches. However, several avenues remain to be explored. Future research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms by which obesity influences CAR-T cell metabolism and function, potentially uncovering novel therapeutic targets. Additionally, long-term follow-up studies are needed to assess the sustained impact of obesity on patient outcomes, including relapse rates and long-term toxicities. The development and validation of personalized treatment protocols, tailored to individual patient characteristics such as body composition and inflammatory profiles, could further optimize CAR-T therapy outcomes.

By integrating these insights into clinical practice, it is possible to not only mitigate the risks associated with CAR-T therapy but also to maximize its efficacy for a broader range of patients, including those who are obese.
